Drought Continues to Plague Northern Plains

Thu Aug 10, 2017 at 06:00 AM
The severe drought in the Northern Plains continues to put a strain on
livestock and crop producers, forcing farmers and ranchers to find ways to
utilize what little crops they can produce, find creative ways to feed their
livestock, or make critical decision to downsize or liquidate their herds.
And, based on the most recent U.S. Drought Monitor
(http://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/), there is no end in sight.

According to Jim Honeyman, FSA District Director, who also happens to be
a livestock producer in the southwestern part of North Dakota, it has been
an abnormal year for weather and precipitation. While snowfall was
normal, there was little snowpack which didn’t help subsoil moisture, and
pastures suffered. His area has seen above normal temperatures, with
several days topping 100 degrees, combined with heavy wind.

In South Dakota, FSA Conservation Program Manager, Owen Fagerhaug,
echoes the conditions his northern neighbors are facing. The drought area
continues to increase. Small rain events have provided some relief, but
not enough.

“The grass is very short and dried up. Folks are really struggling,” said
Fagerhaug.

https://inside.fsa.usda.gov/fsa-internal-newsletter/2017/q3/drought-continues-to-the-plague...  8/22/2017

[PDF page 28]
Drought Continues to the Plague Northern Plains  Page 2 of 5

FSA has taken steps to help.

This summer, USDA authorized emergency grazing on Conservation
Reserve Program (CRP) land  (https://www.usda.gov/media/press-
releases/2017/06/23/usda-authorizes-emergency-grazing-drought-
stricken-montana-north)  in Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota.
This includes emergency grazing of CRP land for any county whose border
lies with 150 miles of a county approved for emergency CRP grazing.
Contract holders who harvested their CRP land for hay as part of their
mid-contract management plans, can also donate hay to livestock
producers.

USDA also began allowing producers in North Dakota and South Dakota to
institute emergency haying and grazing, and released additional land
(https://www.usda.gov/media/press-releases/2017/07/20/usda-opens-
more-land-emergency-haying-and-grazing), including wetland and buffer
practices, to be emergency hayed or grazed.

“These emergency actions came at just the right time for livestock
producers,” said Honeyman.

“It will add the forage into the supply chain and allow it to be more
affordable in areas that are short on feed and make the product available
to those who need it,” Fagerhaug said. “It creates more product out there
and alleviates the stress on the market.”

Fagerhaug said many farmers are chopping corn already for silage, but
what in a normal year would produce 15 to 18 tons of silage per acre will
be closer to three tons to the acre this year.

Grain farmers are feeling the heat as well. Honeyman said canola yields
are down and the corn and sunflower crops are not faring well. And in
North Dakota, they are baling the spring wheat for hay

“It’s pretty dismal as far as the crops go,” Honeyman said. “Our yields are
going to be way down.”

https://inside.fsa.usda.gov/fsa-internal-newsletter/2017/q3/drought-continues-to-the-plague...8/22/2017

[PDF page 29]
Drought Continues to the Plague Northern Plains  Page 3 of 5

In addition to the livestock feed concerns, both Honeyman and Fagerhaug
said the water quality for some livestock producers has become
problematic due to high sulfates in the water. The high sulfate
concentration can lead to cattle blindness and even death. Some
producers have been hauling water to their animals as a result, which
Honeyman said, can be a full-time job.

The dry conditions also make it prime for wildfires, adding to the concern
of producers who are wary of sparking a fire while out harvesting hay.

Parts of North Dakota and Montana have experienced fires, including one
in eastern Montana that destroyed over 270,000 acres, according to the
National Interagency Fire Center  (https://inciweb.nwcg.gov/).

Farmers are waiting for the rains to come, but it will probably be too late
as pastures won’t be able to bounce back.

“It’s not going to be a quick fix,” Honeyman said. “Even if it does rain, our
hay and pastures aren’t going to do much. But our farmers are resilient.
They don’t give up easy. They’re going to fight it until they can’t
anymore.”

USDA and FSA staff have a history of helping producers fight to stay in
business and that hasn’t changed. Both Honeyman and Fagerhaug said
offices are very busy working with producers wanting to release CRP
ground for haying and grazing. Other disaster programs, including
Livestock Forage Disaster Program (LFP), Emergency Assistance for
Livestock, Honeybees and Farm-Raised Fish (ELAP), will add to the
workload.

“We are a service agency, and always there to help” Fagerhaug said. “We
are in those communities, and our employees take pride in what we do.”

FSA to the Rescue - Customers Hit Hard by Wildfires

Thu May 4, 2017 at 07:00 AM
In early March, wildfires scorched parts of northwest Oklahoma, southwest
Kansas, the Texas Panhandle and parts of Colorado. In total, the fires
destroyed over 1.5 million acres and an estimated 20,000 head of
livestock perished.

FSA employees in those states were on-hand to provide assistance to
producers during this devastating time. They implemented critical
programs such as the Emergency Conservation Program (ECP), Livestock
Indemnity Program (LIP), Emergency Assistance for Livestock Honeybees
and Farm-Raised Fish Program (ELAP), and the Emergency Grazing on
Conservation Reserve Program (CRP).

After the fires settled, Morgan Bourquin, program technician from
Hemphill County, Texas, assessed the fire damage and made personal
contact with affected producers.

“It’s as bad as you can imagine and maybe even a little worse,” Bourquin
said. “It’s hard for people who haven’t seen it to imagine. It’s people’s
livelihood and their passion, and it was gone within seconds.”

https://inside.fsa.usda.gov/fsa-internal-newsletter/may-04-2017/fsa-to-the-rescue-customer...  8/22/2017

[PDF page 34]
FSA to the Rescue -  Customers Hit Hard by Wildfires  Page 2 of 4

In Clark County, Kansas where it is estimated that 350,000 acres, or 85
percent of the county, burned, FSA held an informational meeting for
producers and nearly 500 showed up. FSA has already processed $1.5M in
LIP payments and continues to utilize the ECP to provide cost-share
assistance to rebuild fences. T.C. Dawson, county executive director for
Kiowa and Clark/Comanche Counties in Kansas, reported that he has one
operation that has lost up to 300 miles of fence.

In addition to the assistance FSA provides, farmers, ranchers and others
from across the country have stepped up to provide much needed hay,
milk replacer and fencing supplies to these states. A feed store in Ashland,
Kansas, serves as a drop off point for many of these donations. Dawson
said the feed store tracked the donations and they reported receiving
donations from every state in the lower 48.

“You can’t drive down the highway without seeing a load of hay with an
American flag on it,” Dawson said.

In Oklahoma, Joy Alspach, chief of the conservation section for Oklahoma
FSA, said they hosted two public meetings, reaching a total of 289
producers. “To walk in and to see the defeated look on producers’ faces
was not easy. Some of those people lost everything - their home, their
cattle, all the grass for their livestock,” Alspach said. “That forage was
crucial to their cattle operation and it’s all gone. The burned pastures will
need a rest period to recover and prevent damage to the grass stand.”

Dawson said there will be a negative financial impact for the affected
producers for several years to come due of the severity of loss.

“ECP and LIP help, but the financial burden is still going to be there.
Guys are going to end up feeding cattle through the summer, where
typically that wouldn’t be a cost,” Dawson said. “Also time and labor
of feeding cattle all summer that typically you wouldn’t have the
labor expense of feeding them every day. Financially, this is going to
be a multi-year situation to recover.”

https://inside.fsa.usda.gov/fsa-internal-newsletter/may-04-2017/fsa-to-the-rescue-customer...  8/22/2017

[PDF page 35]
FSA to the Rescue -  Customers Hit Hard by Wildfires  Page 3 of 4

Through this tragedy, the FSA community has pulled together in an effort
to serve producers as swiftly as possible. Dawson said the
Clark/Comanche office, a shared management office, only has two
program technicians, but Kansas FSA has rallied around them and
volunteers have signed up through June to come and lend a hand.

“I’ve never worked for other government agencies, but that’s
something that I find remarkable about FSA,” Dawson said. “We have
had two to three extra people in the office every week since this
process started helping out, so the producers can get the services as
quickly as possible.”

Alspach echoed that the county office staff in Oklahoma have worked very
hard and have endured the emotional impact of seeing how this disaster
has impacted their friends and neighbors.

“They are the backbone and they are the ones that have been there
working hard to assist the producers,” Alspach said.

Our New Secretary is Here and Hitting the Ground Running!

Thu May 4, 2017 at 07:00 AM
Sonny Perdue, became our 31st Secretary last week and he has hit the
ground running. Secretary Perdue brings a lifetime of experience and
dedication to Agriculture and to improving the lives of farmers, ranchers
and producers, FSA's lifeblood. His will be a powerful voice as he tirelessly
advocates for rural America.

Secretary Perdue is solutions-minded and a man of action, with a
customer-first mentality. Under his leadership, we will work together to
remove roadblocks and strengthen Rural America.

A former farmer, agribusinessman, veterinarian, state legislator and
Governor of Georgia, Secretary Perdue’s strong agricultural background
has helped to prepare him to lead USDA.

At his Senate hearing, Secretary Perdue outlined four guiding principles
that will inform his policies as USDA Secretary:

1.  Maximize the ability of the men and women of America’s agriculture
and agribusiness sector to create jobs, to produce and sell the foods
and fiber that feed and clothe the world, and to reap the earned
reward of their labor;

https://inside.fsa.usda.gov/fsa-internal-newsletter/may-04-2017/our-new-secretary-is-here-...  8/22/2017

[PDF page 57]
Our New Secretary is Here and Hitting the Ground Running!  Page 2 of 5

2.  Prioritize customer service every day for American taxpayers and
consumers;
3.  As Americans, we should expect a safe and secure food supply; and
4.  Always remember that America’s agricultural bounty comes directly
from the land. And today, those land resources sustain more than 320
million Americans and countless millions more around the globe.

More than anything in his life, it was the family farm which shaped
Secretary Perdue. He has lived and breathed the exhilaration of a great
crop and the despair and devastation of a drought. He learned by
experience what his father told him as a child, “If you take care of the
land, the land will take care of you.”

“The only legacy that I seek is the one that any grandparent or
parent seeks – to be good stewards, and to hand off our nation, our
home, our fields, our forests, and our farms to the next generation in
better shape than we found it,”  Secretary Perdue said. “Making sure
that Americans who make their livelihoods in the agriculture industry
have the ability to thrive will be one of my top priorities. I am
committed to serving the customers of USDA, and I will be an
unapologetic advocate for American agriculture.”

Secretary Perdue's first day on the job was definitely a busy one. He and
his wife Mary attended his swearing-in ceremony at the White House,
followed by a warm welcome and opening remarks to his new USDA team
(over 100,000 strong). Secretary Perdue then joined President Trump for
a “Farmers Roundtable  (https://www.usda.gov/media/press-
releases/2017/04/25/perdue-joins-white-house-farmers-roundtable-
president-trump-issues)”  at the White House to address issues facing the
American agriculture community, as the president signed an Executive
Order establishing an Interagency Task Force on Agriculture and Rural
Prosperity  (https://www.whitehouse.gov/the-press-

‘The Farmer’s Roundtable’ at the White House featured more than a dozen
farmers and representatives from all corners of American agriculture, who
gathered to discuss topics such as agricultural trade, regulatory reform,
rural investment and infrastructure, labor issues and the farm bill. This,
just as the task force begins its mission “to promote economic
development and revitalization, job growth, infrastructure, innovation, and
quality of life issues for rural America.”

“The people who are on the front lines of American agriculture don’t
have the luxury of waiting to tend to their crops and livestock, so
there was no better time to convene this meeting of the minds than
on my first day,”  Secretary Perdue said. “President Trump has made
it clear that addressing the needs of rural America will be a top
priority, and the message that we want to send to the agriculture
community is that we are here, we are working hard, and we are on
their side. The Farmers Roundtable provided the chance for the
President to hear directly from the people on the front lines of
American agriculture about what they are dealing with every day. By
hosting this discussion, the president has demonstrated his
awareness of the plight of American farmers, ranchers, foresters, and
producers, his intention to seek input, and his determination to help.”

(his official handle is @SecretarySonny)

## Contest Rating & Badge



The contest badge is calculated based on the contest rating.

For LeetCoders with rating >=1600, If you are in the top 5% of the contest rating, you’ll get the “Guardian” badge.

If you are in the top 25% of the contest rating, you’ll get the “Knight” badge.

## Contest Rating & Badge



The contest badge is calculated based on the contest rating.

For LeetCoders with rating >=1600, If you are in the top 5% of the contest rating, you’ll get the “Guardian” badge.

If you are in the top 25% of the contest rating, you’ll get the “Knight” badge.

AP Capstone Policy on Use of Generative Artificial
Intelligence (AI)

DEFINITION OF GENER ATIVE AI IN AP CAPSTONE COURSES
Generative AI tools use predictive technology to produce new tex t , char ts, images, audio, video,
etc. This includes not only ChatGPT and similar Large Language Models (LLMs), but also many
writing assistants or plug -ins that are built on this or similar AI technologies.

POLICY ON ACCEPTABLE GENER ATIVE AI USE IN AP CAPSTONE COURSES
Generative AI tools must be used ethically, responsibly, and  intentionally to suppor t student
learning, not to bypass it . Accordingly, all per formance tasks submitted in AP Seminar and AP
Research must be the student’s own work . While students are permitted to use generative AI tools
consistent with this policy, their use is optional and not mandator y.

Students can use generative AI tools as optional aids for exploration of potential topics of
inquir y, initial searches for sources of information, confirming their understanding of a complex
tex t , or checking their writing — but not rewriting — for grammar and tone. However, students
must read primar y and secondar y sources directly, per form their own analysis and synthesis of
evidence, and make their own choices on how to communicate effectively both in their writing
and presentations. Students may not use generative AI tools to write or create their assignments
for them. It remains the student’s responsibilit y to engage deeply with credible, valid sources and
integrate diverse perspectives when working on the per formance tasks. Students must complete
interim “checkpoints” with their teacher to demonstrate genuine engagement with the tasks.

Hyper tension

High blood pressure (hyper tension) is one of the leading causes of cardiovascular
disease.139 Several studies demonstrate that the more social suppor t one has, the
greater the reduction in the possibilit y of developing high blood pressure, even
in populations who are at higher risk for the condition, such as Black Americans.
Greater social suppor t in this group is associated with a 36% lower risk of high

on hyper tension risk is even greater than that of other major clinical risk factors
such as diabetes.59

REQUIRED CHECKPOINTS AND AFFIRMATIONS
To ensure students are not using generative AI to bypass work , students must complete interim
“checkpoints” with their teacher to demonstrate genuine engagement with the tasks. AP Seminar
and AP Research students will need to complete the relevant checkpoints successfully
to receive a score for their per formance tasks. Teachers must affirm, to the best of their
knowledge, that students completed the checkpoints authentically in the AP Digital Por t folio.
Failure to complete the checkpoints will result in a score of zero on the associated task.

§  In AP Seminar, teachers assess the authenticit y of student work based on checkpoints that
take the form of shor t conversations with students during which students make their thinking
and decision-making visible (similar to an oral defense). These checkpoints should occur during
the sources and research phase (IRR and IWA), and argument outline phase (IWA only).
§  In AP Research, students must complete “checkpoints” in the form of in-progress meetings and
work in the Process and Reflection Por t folio (PREP).
AP Seminar and AP Research teachers are also required to affirm, to the best of their knowledge,
that the student’s final submission is authentic student work .
